text:
The webhook edge faces the public internet, so its order is its security
argument. The path segment is text a stranger sent: net/http decodes %00 in
it to a NUL byte and hands over 500 bytes of anything just as happily. So
the segment is resolved to a registered provider before a byte of the body
is read, an unknown one is answered 404 with nothing stored, and everything
downstream is handed the registry's own key. That is what makes
outbox.Delivery.Provider a constant of the program: outbox.Accept refuses an
unstorable provider with an error that is deliberately not a sentinel,
because it treats a bad provider as a caller bug and not as poison, and a
caller that passed request text there would turn a crafted URL into a 500
and a provider into a retry storm.

The registry validates a key by calling record.ValidProviderKey rather than
by carrying a copy of the pattern. ADR 3 freezes the grammar, the same
string is the first segment of every scope id and of every external id, and
a registry that accepted "ms-graph" would register a provider whose every
record fails in Seal, far from here. A test holds the two functions to the
same verdict on every byte in the first and in a later position.

The body is captured once, under an http.MaxBytesReader that sits in front
of everything that touches it, hashing included, and those exact bytes go to
the handshake hook, to verification and on to the hub. Re-serialized JSON
never matches a provider's HMAC, so the acceptance test signs a body whose
re-serialization differs and the control case, the same signature over the
re-serialized bytes, answers 401. A body with no end is cut at the cap
instead of being accumulated, and an announced Content-Length may size one
buffer but never reserve more than a megabyte, since it is a claim and not a
promise.

The response codes are the contract, because a provider acts on them
thousands of times: 401 only for a signature failure, 2xx for everything
else including parked poison, 413 over the cap, 400 for a body that stopped,
and 503 with a Retry-After when the accept runs out of time. That last one
is how a saturated connection pool answers instead of hanging: every accept
holds one of pgxpool's max(4, NumCPU) connections, so the accept is bounded
and pool_max_conns is documented where an operator reads it.

Registrar, Reconciler and MemberSource are deliberately not written yet.
Subscription, Credential, Cursor and ScopeMembers are decided by B07, B13,
B14, B19 and B23, and an interface written before its types are settled is a
shape every later item rewrites. Architecture section 7 says so.

serve does not mount the edge yet. An edge with no hub would answer a
provider without storing anything, so ingress.New refuses a nil hub, and
B07 does the wiring along with the hub itself.

Closes #6
title: Put a provider behind the ingress edge before anything is read

text:
The head-of-key rule only looked at the earliest unfinished row, so two versions of one entity
could be leased together, and the later one delivered first:

- Late commit. seq is assigned at INSERT, not at COMMIT. v1 could be inserted first and commit
  last; a claim in between leased v2, and the next one leased v1 alongside it. Accept now takes a
  transaction-scoped advisory lock on a hash of (tenant, ordering key) before the INSERT, so
  within one key, seq order is commit order.
- Replay. v1 dead, v2 in flight, Replay(v1) made v1 the head again. A replayed row now takes a
  fresh seq under the same lock and goes to the BACK of its key's queue. A lease check alone would
  still race, because it runs on the claim's snapshot; a row that is behind cannot.

The claim also re-checks seq on the locked row (it may have been replayed between the snapshot and
the row lock), and as a second line of defense a key is not eligible while any other unfinished
row of it holds a live lease.

Also from the review:

- clip made the stored cause valid (UTF-8, no NUL, cut between runes). Postgres rejected the
  statement otherwise, so the failure was never recorded and the row looped at lease cadence.
- Replay restores prepared for a row that died after it was prepared (new prepared_at column), so
  it is delivered again but not prepared again.
- The state re-check on the locked row, and the new seq re-check, are now pinned by deterministic
  tests: a test-only BEFORE UPDATE trigger pauses the claim on an advisory lock after its snapshot
  and before it locks the later rows.
- The worker role no longer has SELECT on lease_token. It only writes it.

The migration is edited in place: it has not been merged or released.
title: B04 review round 1: one version of an entity in flight, under every interleaving

author: gablooge
text:
The first cycle ran three reviews and three fixes in parallel on
stacked pull requests, and found four blocking bugs. What it taught:

- Parallel implementers are fine in isolated worktrees, one branch
  each. The orchestrator then owns the merge-forward, in stack order.
- A branch checked out in another worktree needs a detached HEAD and
  an explicit push refspec.
- The session scratchpad is shared between agents. Temporary files
  belong in the agent's own worktree.
- A mutation that makes a test hang is a defect in the test.
- On a re-review, replies are claims. Re-run the reproductions and the
  surviving mutations, and treat the fix as new code.
- A correctness argument is attacked by experiment: EXPLAIN, forced
  plans, a stress test that is itself checked against a mutant.
- Approved with a should-fix on isolation, secrets, ordering or a
  surviving mutation: fix it before moving on. Notes for later items
  go onto those items' issues.
- A pull request description is updated when the design changes.

Also ignore .claude/worktrees/.
title: Agents: lessons from the first review cycle

author: gablooge
text:
Two defects on this branch had one cause: a check reading the pattern
string where net/http reads the parsed pattern. The pattern parser
percent-decodes a literal segment before it stores it, so the string a
check sees is not the string the mux matches with.

Route.check compared the raw Path against the webhook prefix, so
"/%69ngress/fake" and "/ingres%73/fake" walked past it and were stored
as the pattern "/ingress/fake", answering every delivery for that
provider in the edge's place with nothing logged. And the redirect probe
asks about one representative path per pattern, using the pattern string
as that path, so a wildcard is asked about as the literal text "{x}":
"/a/%7Bx%7D" is stored as exactly that literal, matches the
representative, and a table of POST /a/{x}/ plus that route reported "no
redirect" while POST /a/b still answered 307 over a socket.

Route.Path now refuses a percent-escape outright rather than decoding
one. It closes both at once, it costs a caller nothing (a Route is a Go
string literal in this repository's own source), and it is what makes
the written path and the parsed pattern the same string for every check
in the package. It also made the probe's RawPath handling unreachable,
so that is gone, along with a comment about EscapedPath that was wrong:
EscapedPath turns an undecodable "/a/%zz" into "/a/%25zz" rather than
leaving it as written. The Route.Path doc no longer claims the prefix is
refused "whatever it is spelled as", because it was not.

Three mutants that survived at 100% statement coverage now have tests.
The "< 400" bound on what counts as a redirect: reading a 405 as one
registers a guard where none belongs and turns the mux's own 405 and its
Allow header into this package's "no such provider" 404. The trailing
slash on edgePrefix: without it "/ingress", "/ingressive" and
"/ingressX/y" are all refused, and nothing asserted what stays accepted.
And a conflict in the second guard route rather than the first, which
was only covered for the first.

The fourth, clearing "guarding" after a guard is registered, is an
equivalent mutant and is marked at the line instead: the name is
reassigned unconditionally immediately before the only calls that can
panic while it is read, so a stale value can never be reported. The two
the review already judged equivalent are marked the same way.

New can refuse a routing table net/http accepts, when a method-less
subtree meets a method-specific sibling at the same depth. The refusal
is right and the message is good, but nothing said it could happen. New,
Route and architecture 3.1 now say so and give the way out: name the
method on the subtree route. B08 is the caller that will meet it.

The backlog's round 4 line claimed the probe is "exact by construction
for every pattern spelling". It is not, and the finding above is the
counterexample: it is exact for the one path it asks about. The line is
corrected in place.
title: Read the path net/http stores, not the path a Route writes

text:
net.SplitHostPort only checks the shape, so Load accepted any value with
exactly one colon as SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR. The listener then looked the
"port" up as a service name and its error, which run logs, quoted it:
"leakuser:hunter2" logged "lookup tcp/hunter2: unknown port", and a
database URL with no password and no port logged the URL. That is the
very thing the check was added to prevent.

Two changes, because the port and the host are separate holes:

Load now requires the port to be a number from 0 to 65535. This
deliberately stops accepting service names such as ":http", which
nothing here needs. The strconv error quotes its input, so it is not
wrapped.

A numeric port says nothing about the host, and "leakhost:8080" is a
legitimate shape, so serve no longer returns the net error at all. It
keeps only what cannot carry the address: the errno (wrapped alone, so
"address already in use" and "permission denied" survive and
errors.Is(err, syscall.EADDRINUSE) still works), the context error, or
the DNS error's classification. Anything else is a fixed message. Every
message names the variable.

Tests: the single-colon and out-of-range cases in the config tests, a
list of ordinary addresses that must still load, a run-level test that
drives serve with a host that does not resolve (.invalid) and an address
no interface carries (<ip>/24), both offline and under a deadline,
a real bind conflict that must still say "in use" without the address,
and a table over every error shape listenError can be given.
title: Review round 2: the listen address cannot reach the log either

author: gablooge
text:
Three findings from the round 2 review of the store, each reproduced with a failing test first.

The preflight accepted a login holding ADMIN OPTION on a helper role. USAGE is false and SET is
true in that state, so Open passed, and the application role could then grant itself the helper
role WITH INHERIT TRUE while running. The preflight now also requires
pg_has_role(helper, 'MEMBER WITH ADMIN OPTION') to be false. Postgres answers the USAGE and SET
spellings identically (all are is_admin_of_role, which follows memberships whether or not they
are inherited), and that reach is wanted: the new table cases show the escalation both directly
and through a role the login can only SET ROLE to.

The bootstrap did not always leave the administrator with what it started with. Membership rows
are keyed by grantor, so borrowing SET rewrote an existing self-granted row that lacked SET
(createrole_self_grant = 'inherit' makes one) and the REVOKE then deleted it. ALTER SCHEMA ...
OWNER TO needs the same SET on Postgres 16 and 17, so the borrow cannot be avoided. The script
now borrows only when the schema is missing and SET is lacking, records the administrator's rows
first, and afterwards restores the row that changed or revokes the row that is new, with the
grantor Postgres picked. A new test pins the exact rows for five starting states, including an
administrator that has SET but no ADMIN OPTION, which is what makes "always borrow" fail.

A schema "sluiceway" owned by another role was accepted silently and Migrate then failed with a
misleading 3F000. The preflight now compares the owner with the login role and returns
ErrSchemaNotOwned, a sentinel of its own: isolation is not at stake, so it is not ErrUnsafeRole,
and running the bootstrap again does not change an existing schema's owner, so
ErrNotBootstrapped would point the wrong way. The bootstrap script raises a clear error (55000)
in the same situation, before changing anything.

Architecture section 4 and ADR 2 describe all of this, and state that the preflight runs once
per process.
title: B03 review round 2: refuse ADMIN OPTION, restore the admin's membership, refuse a foreign schema

author: gablooge
text:
The head marker made the isolation level load-bearing, and nothing asked for it. A writer of a
key waits for the key's advisory lock and then decides from what it can see. Under READ COMMITTED
its next statement takes a new snapshot and sees what the previous holder committed. Under
REPEATABLE READ the snapshot is the transaction's, taken by the set_config that binds the tenant,
before the wait: an Accept behind an open MarkDelivered still sees version 1 unfinished and stores
version 2 without the marker, a finish behind an open Accept promotes nothing, and a Replay does
what Accept does. The key is left with unfinished rows and no head, Claim returns nothing for it
forever, and no error is raised. One ALTER DATABASE or ALTER ROLE is enough to get there.

store.begin, the one place the application opens a transaction, now begins it READ COMMITTED by
name, so a default on the server, the database or the role cannot change it. The preflight runs
single statements and goose opens its own transactions for DDL under Migrate's session lock, so
neither matters. ADR 10, architecture 3.2 and the doc comment of begin say so. The three
lost-promotion tests now run on databases whose default is REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, and a
store test checks the level inside every transaction helper with the default set on the database
and on the role. Without the fix all of them fail (the outbox ones with "0 heads among 1
unfinished rows" under REPEATABLE READ and SQLSTATE 40001 under SERIALIZABLE).

A database error inside finishIn read as ErrLeaseLost survived the whole suite, because the test
for that property cancels its context before the transaction begins. TestAFailedFinishIsNotALostLease
makes each of the three statements fail for a reason that is not the lease (the key's lock, by
cancelling once the finish is seen waiting behind an open Accept, the state change and the
promotion by a throwaway trigger), for MarkDelivered, MarkDead and Fail to dead, and wants a
wrapped error, unchanged rows and the same lease working afterwards. finishIn is at 100 percent.

An ordering key with a NUL or invalid UTF-8 came back as the database's SQLSTATE 22021, which the
ingress cannot tell from an outage: a retry storm from one crafted entity id, since encoding/json
decodes the escape for U+0000 into that byte. It is ErrBadOrderingKey now, refused before the
database is asked. The provider (a constant of the program, not sender-controlled) is refused in
words as well, and an id that no row can have is ErrNotFound in Get and Replay.

Every row of ADR 10's window table has a deterministic test now, named next to it: leased inside
the window, given a backoff inside the window (both rest on re-checking a STORED generated column,
and both fail, under all five planner settings, against a claim that judges due_at through a join),
replayed onto an empty key (leased, rightly), and a locked row (skipped, not waited for).

Outbox.StrandedKeys finds the one broken state that is silent: a key with unfinished rows and no
head. It is scoped to a tenant, because the worker role reads neither state nor ordering_key and
that is not widened here. ADR 10 has the repair statement, and the test runs it. The sweep and the
metric are B25.

ADR 10 gave 260 dead index entries per page as if it were the rate. It is the best case (pages
filled in index order). Measured one row at a time: 8.7 pages per 1,000 deliveries here, 11 in the
review. The record also takes the review's 20 percent for the write path as a whole.
title: B04 review of the redesign: ask for READ COMMITTED, and close three gaps in the tests

author: gablooge
text:
The review of bd28237 found the rename itself sound and four small
things.

Two are whitespace a blind replacement disturbed: the cmd row of the
package layout, and a continuation line in the bootstrap header that an
administrator reads before running the script as superuser.

The credentials table named a Cloudflare token variable after the
maintainer's own domain. A public repository does not need that; the
convention is what matters.

The rest was three places telling three different stories about who can
read this. CLAUDE.md said private until v0.1.0 while a paragraph below
it reasoned from the repository being public, and the roadmap promised
a flip at M6. The decision changed on 2026-09-20: public from the
record format onward, because the work is worth reading before it is
worth running. CLAUDE.md now states the rule that follows from it
rather than a date, so it stays true either way.

The SECURITY.md finding is a repository setting, not a code change:
private vulnerability reporting is turned on in the same step that
makes the repository public. The remaining finding belongs to the
follow-up commit that renames the record format once B05 lands.
title: Review of the rename: alignment, a personal token name, and one story about visibility

The delta review of edeba03 found nothing blocking, but two mutations survived: removing
scrub from begin (behind Tx, TenantTx and RoleTx), and removing it from Migrate. Every leak
test went through Open, which fails in its preflight and never reaches either. The pool

"failed to connect to user=... database=...: dial tcp host:port", and a rewrite of begin
could have put that back into the log with a green suite.

TestALostDatabaseNeverEchoesTheURL opens a pool through an in-process TCP forwarder in
front of the test database, cuts the forwarder after Open, and asserts for Tx, TenantTx,
RoleTx and Migrate that the error names SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL, still matches
syscall.ECONNREFUSED, and carries no part of the URL at any depth of its chain. The call
that meets the dead pooled connection is checked for leaks as well. Both mutations now fail.

connect_timeout=0 means "wait forever" to libpq, but pgx parses it to the same zero as a
missing parameter, so it gets the 10 second default. That is the safe reading and it stays,
now on purpose: the constant's comment and architecture section 4 say so, and
TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout has the row.

scrub judges the error, not where it came from, so a net error that a transaction function
returns is replaced too, with whatever the function wrapped around it. Kept, deliberately:
a statement that fails inside the function on a dead connection is returned by the function
and does carry the address, and telling it from a net error of the caller's own would rest
on a pgx side channel on every failure path, where a miss leaks the connection target. A
wrong label, in a case the architecture forbids anyway (no network I/O inside a
transaction), costs less than that. Documented on begin, Tx, TenantTx, RoleTx and scrub and
in section 4, and pinned by TestANetErrorFromTheTransactionFunctionIsReplacedToo.

The comments on the two cancellation tests now say that they pin pgxpool behaviour, that no
mutation of this package can fail them, and that they exist to notice a pgx upgrade. The
first scrub in Migrate is unreachable today (goose connects in Up, not in NewProvider), and
a comment says why it stays.

text:
A failure is recorded as an outbox.Cause, never as text. Fail and
MarkDead took a string, and the obvious call is err.Error(): the error
of an HTTP client quotes the request URL, and the query string is where
many sinks and providers carry their API key. last_error is a plain
column that operators read and every backup carries. A Cause is one of
the outbox's own classifications, an HTTP status, and the remote error
code only if it looks like one, otherwise "withheld". There is no
constructor that takes an error or a message. dead_reason is one of two
fixed texts. clip stays, as the last line of defense, with a unit test
of its own. The rule is on the columns in the migration and in
architecture 3.2.

Claimed is read-only (ID, Tenant, Attempt). A genuine lease aimed at
another tenant already changed nothing, because row-level security hides
the row, and that is now tested with a real token, where tenant B even
has a row of the same entity under it. Outside the package such a value
can no longer be written at all.

An ordering key is at most 512 bytes, in Accept (ErrBadOrderingKey, for
the ingress to park as poison and answer 2xx) and as a CHECK. A longer
key failed the INSERT or not depending on how well it compressed, as an
opaque database error the caller could not tell from an outage. The
error reports the length, not the key.

Claim's refusal of a batch or lease that is not positive is tested: a
lease of zero would use up the ladder with no delivery ever tried. Its
cap is MaxBatch, documented and tested against 1,005 claimable keys.

A database or context error is never reported as ErrLeaseLost or
ErrNotFound, tested with a cancelled context through every entry point:
the two tell a worker opposite things.

sqlc omits unused structs: outboxdb.Outbox was the one type pairing
raw_body with lease_token, and nothing used it or outboxdb.Tenant.

The backlog log line is brought up to date for rounds 2 and 3, and no
longer recommends the trigger technique that round 2 showed to fail.

The first routing rule allowed [a-z0-9_-]{1,64} as the path segment,
and the text here called that the shape of a provider key. ADR 3, which
arrived with the record format, freezes the provider segment of a scope
id as a lowercase letter followed by up to 31 lowercase letters, digits
or underscores. A registry built from the looser rule would accept a
key such as ms-graph, and every record of that provider would then fail
to seal.

Cloudflare now forwards only ^/ingress/[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$, checked
again from the public internet: a hyphen, a leading digit, a capital
and a 33 character key are all refused there.
title: Tunnel rule: a provider key is ADR 3's grammar, not a looser one

author: gablooge
text:
The rule that decided when to register the slash-less route compared path
strings, and whether net/http.ServeMux redirects is a property of the whole
routing table. It was wrong in both directions.

It buried a caller's route. With POST /v1/{resource} and POST /v1/tenants/ on
the table, a bare mux answers POST /v1/tenants from the wildcard with no
Location, because an exact match stops the redirect before it starts. The
string rule saw no route whose path was "/v1/tenants", registered the 404
anyway, and a literal beats a wildcard: one path out of a family answered "no
such provider" with nothing logged.

And it refused a table net/http accepts. GET /v1/{id}/ plus GET /v1/{name}
made it register GET /v1/{id}, which conflicts, so New failed at start quoting
a pattern the caller never wrote.

The table is fully built before the answer is needed, so New now builds a
second mux carrying the same patterns and handlers that do nothing, and serves
a synthetic request into that one. Nothing a caller wrote can run, the answer
is exact by construction for every pattern spelling, and the deduplication of
two routes with one root falls out of it: the second route sees the first
route's guard as an exact match.

That also removes the enumeration of "three spellings", which was incomplete.
net/http stores a literal last segment written %2F as the same segment as {$},
so Route{POST, "/a/%2F"} was accepted and POST /a answered 307 Location: /a/
through the handler New returns, which is the one thing this package promises
cannot happen.

A route under /ingress/ is refused at start. The duplicate-pattern check
caught POST /ingress/{provider} spelled exactly and nothing else, so
POST /ingress/fake was accepted with no error and no log and answered every
delivery for that provider in the edge's place.

Two mutations the reviewer found surviving are marked at the line as changing
no answer rather than left looking tested: the duplicate-pattern pre-check

text:
The blocking finding of round 1 is that the fake's utf8.Valid check survived
its own mutation. The only fixture naming UTF-8 sent {0xff,0xfe,'}'}, which is
not JSON, so encoding/json refused it either way and the check was never the
thing that refused. Go's JSON scanner accepts any byte above 0x1f inside a
string and the decoder rewrites what is not UTF-8 to U+FFFD, so the case that
matters is a bad byte inside a JSON string, in the one field the double does
not otherwise constrain: title. Six fixtures now carry one there, each asserted
to be valid JSON so nothing but utf8.Valid can refuse it, and deleting the
check fails all six. Hunting the same shape found two more checks whose tests
were satisfied elsewhere: the external id length bound (no fixture was ever too
long) and the UTC normalization of occurred_at (every fixture was already
spelled with a Z). Coverage was 100% throughout and showed none of it.

WebhookSource.Verify now takes a provider.Request rather than body, header and
secret. HubSpot's v3 signature (B18) covers the request method and the full
request URI, and by then B07, B11 and B15 have implemented the interface, so
widening it later costs four packages. A struct rather than more parameters,
because the next scheme to need one more field must not break the ones already
written. DeliveryKeys and Parse keep the body: the routing keys are in the
delivery's own content, and Parse runs in the worker where only the bytes were
stored. Hub.Accept carries the same Request, since the hub is what calls Verify
once per candidate.

The security decision inside that is where the URL comes from. A provider
signed the public URL, which behind the tunnel is not what the Go server sees,
and the obvious sources (Host, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, Forwarded)
are all written by the sender and passed through unchanged. A receiver that
built the signed URL out of them would let the sender choose part of what it is
proving, so the check would pass over content the sender picked. The base is
therefore LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL: validated at start, absolute, no credentials,
no query, no trailing slash, and the edge appends the request's own escaped
path and raw query. config.NormalizePublicBaseURL owns the spelling and
ingress.New calls it rather than copying the rules, because the two strings end
up compared byte for byte inside an HMAC. Unset is a refusal and not a guess:
the edge still serves, Request.URL is empty, and a scheme that signs the URL
returns false. That is loud, and the alternative is a signature checked against
a URL Lawang invented, which passes or fails for reasons nobody can reason
about.

Three smaller holes in the edge. A registered provider that is not a
WebhookSource answers the same 404 as an unregistered one, deliberately, but it
said nothing at all: only our own wiring can reach that branch, and every real
delivery is being dropped where the loss shows up on the provider's dashboard
and nowhere else, so it is logged at warn with the registry's own constant. A
handshake may no longer answer 401 or 403: architecture 3.1 reserves 401 for a
signature that did not verify, a handshake has nothing to verify, and a
provider answering a malformed challenge with 401 would make the one reserved
status ambiguous for whoever reads the table later. And the handshake content
type was checked for shape only, so a provider could answer text/html with an
echoed challenge and the edge would write it verbatim; nosniff does not help
when the declared type really is HTML, so the type is now an allowlist of
text/plain and application/json with at most charset=utf-8, capped at 64 bytes.

Also: the README says plainly that serve does not mount the route until B07,
because a mux 404 and the edge's own 404 are indistinguishable from outside;
printableASCII is written once again, because the content type allowlist
replaced the edge's copy rather than sharing it; and Registry.Keys is gone,
having had no caller and no named future one, while Entry.Provider names B08.
title: Take the URL a signature covers from configuration, not from a header

The envelope a sink receives becomes a public contract at v0.1, so this
settles it before anything produces a record: ADR 3 (scope id) and ADR 4
(field names, what is required, how the format may change).

internal/record holds the Go types, Validate, Seal, the scope id builder
and parser, and the JSON Schema (draft 2020-12), embedded so the binary
and the tests use the same bytes. A record that fails Validate cannot be
marshalled, and a document the schema refuses cannot be unmarshalled, so
the Go side and the schema refuse the same things. About 250 documents,
46 Go values and a fuzz target are run through both.

What differs from the proposal in architecture section 6:

- a "format" field carries the version, because a record outlives any
  media type or file it arrived in;
- meta.raw_ref is dropped: it pointed into a store the design does not
  have;
- "delete" is defined now. op is a closed set, so a value that is only
  reserved could never be added without a new format version;
- visibility is closed, every other object ignores unknown fields, and
  field names are lowercase only, because some decoders (Go's) match
  names without regard to case;
- the scope is hashed into the record id. A task moved to another list
  is decided on other members, and a provider's version need not change
  with a move. With the old recipe the moved record kept its id, the
  ledger skipped it as delivered and the sink kept the old scope, with
  no error anywhere. This changes ids.RecordID and the golden vectors of
  B02, re-verified with the Python blake3 package. Nothing has been
  delivered yet, so re-keying costs nothing today.

The scope id uses the internal provider key and never the wire name: it
is the join key between a record and the membership of its scope, and a
renamed source would otherwise cut every stored record off from its
members. The container id is percent-escaped into one canonical
spelling, so Microsoft Graph ids round-trip and no scope parses two ways.

The README and goal 2 of the architecture said a record carries its
scope's members. It carries the scope only. Members travel through
access sync, which is also why a membership change never needs a record
to be delivered again.

Closes #5
title: B05: record format v1, the scope id, and the scope in the record id

author: gablooge
text:
The record format becomes a public contract at v0.1.0, and by its own rule nothing
in it can be tightened or redefined afterwards. The review found two holes and
eight things that were said but not pinned. All of them are settled here.

Blocking. The tests of "one scope, one spelling" survived four mutants, because
the Go parser and the schema could drift together on an escape no example named
(%61). All 256 bytes as %XX, in four spellings of hex, now go through the parser,
the schema and the decoder and are judged against the rule, not against each
other, and so does every character of the provider and kind segments. The strict
decoder accepted a document that was not UTF-8, and one with half of a surrogate
pair escaped, and encoding/json rewrote both to U+FFFD, so two documents became
one identity while Python refused the first and kept the second apart. Both are
refused on the bytes now, before parsing, and ADR 4 makes it a rule of the format.

Decided now because later is a v2. The compatibility promise is stated from the
reader's side (every record Sluiceway produces validates against every earlier v1
schema), which makes a raised limit or a widened pattern a new version, and ADR 3
no longer calls a hyphen free. Character rules, field by field: identifiers refuse
controls, the line and paragraph separators, bidirectional formatting and the
common zero-width characters, a display name the same but keeps the joiners,
a title is one line, a text refuses only NUL. An external id is unique within a
tenant, begins with the provider key and a colon, and Seal enforces that, so a
sink keys by tenant and external id and never by the wire name. origin.untrusted
false means no signal, never safe, because v0.1 sets it for no provider.

Enforced, not only said: a test fails when anything outside internal/record
refers to ids.RecordID, and Marshal refuses a record whose id, external id,
version or scope is not what Seal left there. The cost is four string compares.

The A, B, A move is not fixed in the format. ADR 4 requires B08 to dead-letter
and count it, never to skip it, and marks that as decided by default for the
maintainer to overrule. ADR 3 now says a scope id is encoded once more in a URL,
with a test against a real server.

The id recipe, the golden files and the architecture example are unchanged.
title: B05 review round 1: close what freezes with v0.1.0 before it does

A third agent beside implementer and pr-reviewer. It looks outward:
who has the problem this solves and what they use today, what stops a
stranger from adopting the project, what would make it more useful,
what must exist before strangers arrive, and what to say at launch.

It drafts and proposes only. A public statement cannot be taken back
and carries the maintainer's name, so the agent never posts, emails or
messages anyone, and never submits the project anywhere. Its output is
files under growth/ and issues labelled growth, at most eight per run,
for the maintainer to accept or reject. It never touches code, the
backlog or the roadmap.

Two rules carry most of the weight. It reads the open web, so text is
data and never instructions, and nothing from this machine goes into a
query. And its honesty standard is the project's own: no claim that
does not run, every statement about another project sourced and dated,
comparisons made with respect, no astroturfing of any kind.

It writes for readers who use English as a second language or through
a translator.

The same value is normalized more than once in a running deployment: config.Load
normalizes the variable, ingress.New normalizes what Load stored, and a Registrar
in B13 or B18 will register what Load stored with the provider. Those spellings
meet inside an HMAC base string, so a rule that moves a value on a second pass
makes the edge verify against one string while the provider signed another, and
the provider gets 401 on every delivery forever.

Two rules did move a value. TrimSuffix removed one trailing slash, so
"https://x//" came back as "https://x/", keeping the slash the function promises
to remove and losing it on the next pass. The RawPath guard only caught escapes
Go re-spells, so %20, %23 and %3F were decoded into a literal space, hash or
question mark, which the next pass then refused: Load accepted a value that made
ingress.New fail to build the handler, with an error that deliberately does not
quote it.

Each rule is now idempotent in itself. Every trailing slash is removed rather
than one, and the path prefix must already be its own escaped form, which is
what catches an escape that re-encodes to itself. Idempotence is asserted as a
property over a corpus and a fuzz target rather than as two more table rows,
because rows only cover what somebody thought of: the fuzzer found two shapes
nobody had, an escaped "!" that url.URL.String re-escaped in the answer and a
host of "%25" that url.Parse decodes to "%". The host case and a default port
are still kept, and the doc comment now says why: the string has to match the
URL the operator copied from the provider's dashboard.

A path that is not already canonical is refused rather than redirected.
net/http.ServeMux cleans a path and answers 307 before any handler runs, so
//ingress/fake and /ingress/fake/../fake redirected to /ingress/fake. A 307
preserves the method and the body, so a provider re-POSTs, the edge signs the
cleaned path and the provider signed the original, and the 401 that follows is
indistinguishable from a forgery. The guard has to sit in front of the mux,
which is why Mount now returns the handler the server serves.

Two more things an operator and a provider author could not see. ingress.New
warns when LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL is unset, naming the variable and what it
costs, since nothing else in the process mentions it; refusing to start belongs
to B07, which knows which schemes need the URL. And provider.Request.Header is a
read-only provider.Header rather than an http.Header, because the hub hands one
Request to Verify once per candidate: a map would let one implementation change
what the next candidate reads, and a comment asking it not to is not a guard.
title: Normalize a public base URL to something normalizing does not move

author: gablooge
text:
The preflight counted pg_auth_members rows that looked right and required
exactly two. That was wrong in both directions. Postgres 16 keeps one
membership row per grantor and inheritance also flows through intermediate
roles, so Open succeeded while the application role inherited a helper role
(GRANT worker TO ops; GRANT ops TO sluiceway, or a second grantor's INHERIT
TRUE row beside the correct one). A plain transaction with no tenant bound
would then have run under the worker's cross-tenant policies. And a correct
setup bootstrapped by two administrators has four rows, which was refused
with a message telling the operator to do what they had already done.

The preflight now asks Postgres the effective question for each helper
role: pg_has_role(helper, 'USAGE') must be false, pg_has_role(helper, 'SET')
must be true. It names the helper role at fault.

None of the helper-role checks had a test. TestOpenRefusesUnsafeHelperRoles
breaks one thing at a time (helper BYPASSRLS, helper SUPERUSER, INHERIT
TRUE, inheritance through an intermediate role, a second grantor's
inheriting row, SET FALSE, membership revoked) and also proves that two
grantors with correct rows are accepted. Roles are cluster-wide, so these
tests get a Postgres container of their own from testdb.NewRawCluster
instead of altering the roles every other test in the process depends on;
each case still restores in t.Cleanup and starts by proving Open succeeds.

The bootstrap script claimed to work for a CREATEROLE administrator but
died at CREATE SCHEMA ... AUTHORIZATION, half applied: such a role holds the
roles it creates WITH ADMIN OPTION only, and the statement needs SET. The
script now takes SET on sluiceway for that one step, only if it lacks it,
and revokes its own grant again, so the administrator ends with what it
started with. It is now a single DO statement, so it applies completely or
not at all under any client. testdb sends it over the extended protocol,
which refuses a second statement, so that property cannot rot silently.
TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin runs it as a non-superuser CREATEROLE
role: refused without CREATE on the database leaving nothing behind, then
applied twice, migrated, the schema owner and the administrator's rights
checked, then re-run by the superuser (four membership rows) and opened.

TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity now also sees materialized views and
foreign tables, which cannot have row-level security, and fails on any that
is not on the allowlist.

docs/architecture.md section 4 and ADR 2 describe the new preflight and the
privileges the bootstrap needs.
title: B03 review round 1: preflight asks pg_has_role, bootstrap works for CREATEROLE

author: gablooge
text:
Lawang is Javanese for door or gate: the thing every change passes through,
and where it is decided who may see it. That is what this service does, so
the name says it.

The rename had to happen now, before the repository becomes public and
before v0.1 freezes the names that reach operators and sinks: the Go module
path, the binary and its usage text, the LAWANG_* environment prefix, the
Postgres schema, the three database roles and the lawang.tenant setting.
Renaming any of those after a release would be a breaking change for
whoever had deployed it. Nothing is deployed yet, so there is no migration
path: an existing local database is dropped and bootstrapped again.

Two things that are not a word swap:

The Cloudflare Tunnel hostname in CLAUDE.md is removed rather than renamed.
It reaches the maintainer machine while the tunnel runs, and publishing it
in a public repository invites traffic to that machine. The section now
shows a placeholder and says the real hostname lives in the maintainer own
notes. Everything else about the tunnel is unchanged, the ingress routing
rule included.

SECURITY.md is added. The repository is about to be public and the whole
claim of this project is access control, so it needs a private way to
report a flaw: GitHub private vulnerability reporting, an honest statement
that this is one maintainer on best effort, and a scope that names what
counts (a record escaping its scope, a tenant reading another tenant, a
credential reaching a log or a fixture, an unauthenticated caller reaching
the operator API).
title: Rename the project from Sluiceway to Lawang

derivation as well as a stale one.

name, and a deliberately wrong path fails the new test with the reason.

text:
The path guard read the decoded path while net/http cleans the escaped
one, so it was wrong in both directions. It refused /ingress/fake%2f%2fx
and /ingress/%2e%2e, which the mux routes to a handler untouched, and it
never saw the mux's second redirect at all: POST /sub still answered 307
to /sub/ through the handler Mount returned. The guard now reads
r.URL.EscapedPath(), which is the string findHandler cleans.

The trailing-slash redirect cannot be guarded against from in front of
the mux, because it depends on the routing table rather than on the
request. So the routing table is this package's: New builds the mux,
takes every other route as an ingress.Route, and for each of the three
pattern spellings that can match a path ending in a slash it registers
the slash-less path itself with the same 404. A subtree route keeps
working, and nothing redirects.

Mount is gone with it. Its return value could be dropped, and
h.Mount(mux); srv.Handler = mux compiles, vets and lints clean while
serving the unguarded mux with all three redirects back. New now returns
the only servable thing this package hands out, and the edge no longer
implements http.Handler, so there is nothing left to mount by hand.

NormalizePublicBaseURL accepted http://:8080, which names a port and no
machine: u.Host carries the port, so the empty-host check never fired,
and the edge would sign a URL with no host in it while the provider
signed the real one. That is a 401 per delivery with nothing to see, the
failure this function exists to prevent. It also accepted an IDN host
while refusing an IDN path prefix; both are refused now, and punycode is
the spelling a provider's dashboard holds.

provider.Request.Body is a rule and not a guarantee, and architecture 7
said otherwise. The slice aliases the edge's buffer, so an implementation
that normalizes it in place changes what every later candidate verifies
and what B07 stores. Only a per-candidate loop can copy it, and the edge
has none, so the document and the type now say what is true and #7
carries the ask with the measured cost.

author: gablooge
text:
internal/store opens the pgx pool, sets search_path to the sluiceway
schema explicitly (the default "$user" entry follows SET ROLE), and
runs a preflight on every start. It refuses a SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS
login, a helper role with either attribute, memberships that are not
INHERIT FALSE, a database that was never bootstrapped, and a server
older than Postgres 16. Tx, TenantTx and RoleTx are the only ways in.

internal/tenancy validates tenant ids and binds one to a transaction
with a transaction-local setting.

The application role cannot create roles, so a one-time bootstrap
script (printed by "sluiceway migrate bootstrap") creates the three
roles and the schema. Migrations then run as the application role,
under a session advisory lock so replicas can migrate concurrently.

Migration 1 adds the tenant_id domain, current_tenant(), and the
tenants table with row-level security enabled and forced. A
transaction-local setting reads back as '' on a pooled connection once
its transaction ends, so current_tenant() maps '' to NULL.

Integration tests run on testcontainers Postgres as the application
role. One of them fails any future table that does not force
row-level security. Checked by mutation: removing FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY fails six tests.

ADRs 1 (sqlc) and 2 (goose, run as the application role) settle two
open decisions.

Closes #3
title: B03: store, migrations, roles, row-level security

author: gablooge
text:
The schema is a contract for validators in any language, and the three
character classes (identifier, displayName, oneLine) did not compile in Ruby:
its engine refuses a two-digit hex escape of 0x80 or above in a UTF-8 pattern,
so a Ruby sink could not load the schema at all. A pattern now escapes ASCII
only and holds U+0080 to U+009F and U+00AD as the characters themselves, which
the file spells as JSON escapes, the way everything above U+00FF already was.
The set of strings did not change: old against new over all 1,112,064 code
points, no disagreement in Go, Python and ECMAScript (both modes), and the new
patterns give the verdict of ADR 4 for every code point in those and in Ruby.
A test refuses the old spelling, and ADR 4 now says that a respelling with
such a proof is wording, not a change to the format, because after v0.1.0
somebody would otherwise argue that this fix was one.

The character test sampled about 1,800 code points, and four drift mutants
outside the sample survived (U+3164 or U+3000 refused on one side only), while
ADR 4 said this part of the grammar is run in full. It is now: each compiled
pattern of the schema against the Go rule and against the ADR's ranges, for
every code point of Unicode. What the rules deliberately do NOT refuse (tag
characters, variation selectors, the Hangul fillers, U+3000, the zero-width
joiner in a display name) is pinned as named accepted cases, so that a later
tightening, which within v1 is a break in either direction, has to delete a
test with a name.

The seal also holds Op and Kind: an upsert turned into a tombstone after Seal
would have gone out under the id of the version it was. Seal keeps the tenant
privately as well, and Record.SealedFor(tenant) lets the stage that delivers
(B08) notice a record sealed for tenant A that is about to go out under tenant
B, which nothing else can, because the tenant is in no field. It fails closed
for a decoded record. The doc comment of Record says what the seal does not
defend against: a type conversion that sheds the methods. It guards against
accidents.

The caller scan for ids.RecordID had three holes: a directory named bin was
skipped at any depth, internal/ids was exempt as a whole (so a one-line
wrapper there handed the recipe on), and go:linkname needs no reference. All
three are closed, and the test says that it is a tripwire and the seal in
Marshal is the guard.

ADR 4 also states that identifiers are never cleaned (removing a character
merges two ids), only author.display and title are, and that an identifier a
sender controls, such as a mail Message-ID, is escaped or hashed injectively by
the normalizer, never cleaned and never passed through raw.
title: B05 review round 2: a schema Ruby can load, and the character rules run in full

one mutation that survived.

An unknown command was still echoed with %q. The first argument is whatever was typed first:
an image whose entrypoint is the bare binary, run with the database URL as its only argument,
printed the password to stderr, which is the container log. The refusal now says "unknown

TestVariablesAreExactlyWhatLoadReads drove four hand-picked environments, so a variable read
only in development with an explicit database URL went unseen. The bases are now the full
cross product of {unset, each accepted value, one refused value} over every documented
variable (1536 Loads, a few milliseconds), built from Variables itself so that a new variable
joins the product or fails the test. The comment says what recording still cannot see.

The usage comment claimed the text cannot drift from Load. Names and defaults were tied,
accepted values were prose in two places. Variable now carries Values, Load validates against
the same slices, the usage text prints them, and a test holds the two together from outside.
One behaviour change follows: SLUICEWAY_LOG_LEVEL takes the four documented names only, and
no longer slog's offsets such as "info+2", which were never documented.

Smaller: help is listed among the commands, the refuseArguments comment stays true once a
later branch adds "migrate bootstrap", and the development default names localhost:5432 and
the database instead of a compose stack that does not exist before B27.

author: gablooge
text:
The reviewer's surviving mutation: Accept taking the ordering key's lock AFTER
the INSERT left the package green, although it brings back the round 1 late
commit. Two pins now, both deterministic:

- TestAcceptsOfOneKeyCommitInQueueOrder also asserts that v2's seq is above
  that of a row accepted while v2 was waiting. With the order swapped v2 has
  its seq before it waits (2 versus 3).
- TestNoVersionIsClaimableWhileAnEarlierOneIsStillToCommit asserts the
  property itself in the one interleaving where the order decides it: a BEFORE
  INSERT trigger stops T1 after v1 has its seq, and no claim may return v2
  until v1 has committed. With the order swapped nobody holds the lock at that
  point, T2 commits, and the claim leases v2.

The gated claim tests no longer depend on the planner. The old pause was a
BEFORE UPDATE trigger, which only opens a window when the claim locks and
updates its rows one at a time. That is a property of the default plan (a
nested loop with the locked subquery on its outer side), not of the claim: with
nested loops off the old test failed on its 30 second guard, as the reviewer
found, and my earlier description of the plan was wrong. The pause is now a
test-only RESTRICTIVE select policy for the worker role whose function waits
when it is shown the gate row: a policy is checked in the scan, below every
row lock, so the window is there under any plan. Both tests now run under five
planner settings (setup can turn planner settings off for a test database),
and the state and seq re-check mutations fail under all five.
title: B04 review round 2: pin the lock-before-INSERT order, and pause the claim plan-independently

author: gablooge
text:
A failed connection returned pgx's error, and the binary logged it. That error
quotes the user, the database, the host and the port, and the server's own
message quotes the role and the database too. The password never appeared, but
the project rule is that an error names the variable and not its value, and the
base branch already fails a test on exactly those fragments. Open, preflight and
helperStates now keep only a classification (does not resolve, refused, timed
out, authentication failed or no such database with the SQLSTATE, TLS, other)
prefixed with SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL, the way listenError does for the listen
address. The pool connects lazily, so a transaction or a migration can also be
the first to meet an unreachable server: Tx, TenantTx, RoleTx and Migrate
replace an error that carries the connection target and leave every other error
(a constraint violation, a failed migration) as the server sent it. Preflight
refusals say "the login role" instead of its name, which is the user half of
the URL.

The doc comments on RoleTx and tenancy.Bind said a bind narrows a transaction
that is inside a helper role. It does not: Postgres ORs permissive policies, so
under sluiceway_worker with a USING (true) policy every tenant stays visible
whatever is bound. A worker written to that comment would have done per-tenant
work with every tenant's rows in reach, and every tenant-table test would have
passed. The comments and architecture sections 3.2 and 4 now say what is true
(claim in one transaction as the worker role, work in a second one under
TenantTx), a test pins what Postgres does, and the transaction RoleTx hands out
refuses Bind with ErrCrossTenantTx, savepoints included.

Tests that had no teeth, or did not exist:
- The empty-string case of the tenant_id domain test accepted 42501, which the
  policy supplies alone. The domain is now asked directly with a cast and must
  answer 23514. Changing {1,64} to {0,64} fails two tests.
- tenancy.Parse and the domain are fed the same 27 boundary strings and must
  agree, so the rule that is written twice cannot drift.
- The Postgres version refusal is a pure function with a table test.
- The migrate command runs end to end: applies, applies nothing the second
  time, refuses a superuser, never logs a part of the URL.
- A panic and a cancelled context on a pool of one connection leave no role and
  no tenant behind. A mutation made the first version of that test hang in
  pool.Close, so the test helper now bounds Close and fails in seconds.
- Every Down section runs to zero and back up as the application role.

Also: a 10 second connect timeout unless the URL sets connect_timeout (a host
that drops packets held migrate for 75 seconds with nothing logged); the goose
session lock is retried every second instead of every five, which takes the
store package from 20.8 s to 9.4 s and stops the k-th replica waiting 5(k-1)
seconds for a lock that is already free; and tenancy.NewContext, FromContext,
ErrNoTenant and DB.Ping are removed, because nothing but their own tests called
them on this branch or on b04-outbox.
title: B03 review round 3: no part of the database URL in an error, and RoleTx refuses a bind

text:
The claim worked out the head of every unfinished key on every poll and
then threw away all but the batch. With 5,000,000 delivered rows present
it took 265 ms and 386,914 buffers to return 10 rows of 100,000 waiting,
4.1 s and two sequential scans of the heap at 1,000,000, and 391 ms to
find that nothing was due in a sink outage. Batch 10 and batch 100 cost
the same. A worker polls once a second from several goroutines, and the
backlog is set by senders and by a sink someone else runs.

The head of an ordering key is now a stored marker, is_head, and the
claim walks a partial index of heads in the order they fall due
(due_at, a generated column: the later of the backoff and the lease) and
stops at its batch. It visits neither the rows behind a head, nor heads
backing off, nor heads other workers hold. The same shapes now take 0.37
ms and 339 buffers, 0.28 ms and 344, and 0.02 ms and 3. ADR 10 has the
measurements, the correctness argument and what was rejected.

Safety is the database's: a unique index allows one head per key, a
CHECK says a head is unfinished, and the claim re-checks the marker on
the row it has locked, so two rows of one key are never in flight
whatever a writer does. That replaces the claim's NOT EXISTS, which was
evaluated on the snapshot, and lets the worker role lose its SELECT on
ordering_key, next_attempt_at, lease_until and state.

Liveness is the writers': Accept and Replay set the marker when their
key has nothing unfinished, and MarkDelivered and MarkDead hand it to
the next row in the same transaction. The two finishing transitions now
take the key's advisory lock as well, before anything else. Without it
an Accept that sees v1 unfinished stores v2 as a non-head while the
finish of v1, which cannot see v2 yet, promotes nothing, and v2 is never
delivered.

The claim deliberately has no condition on the state. The CHECK already
says it, and repeating it made the planner take is_head and the state
for independent, underestimate the heads, and AND in a bitmap of every
waiting row at a batch of 100. Found by measuring, and now pinned.

Tests: the two gated claim tests still run under five planner settings,
with a gate row that is first in line and row-locked, since a gate row
that is never due is no longer read by the index walk. The raw-insert
test became TestAKeyNeverHasTwoHeads. New: the lost promotion from both
sides and against a replay, each with two real transactions; the marker
through every writer; the invariant as one query, checked during and
after the concurrent tests; a randomized stress test with acceptors
paced so that queues run nearly empty, which is where a promotion can be
lost; and a guard that runs the generated claim through EXPLAIN as the
worker role and bounds the buffers of the search and the shape of its
plan. Two tests that took a minute or two to fail under a mutant now
fail in about a second.
title: B04 review round 3: the claim costs its batch, not the backlog

author: gablooge
text:
Migration 2 adds the outbox table with row-level security forced. The
accept insert is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on (tenant_id, delivery_id).
The key is per tenant, not global: two tenants may connect one provider
workspace, and reconciliation synthesizes byte-identical deliveries for
both. Architecture section 5 is updated.

Claim leases the head of each ordering key (its earliest pending or
prepared row) with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, repeating the state and
lease conditions on the locked row so a row changed between snapshot
and lock is re-checked. A claim is a lease with a token, because the
work spans two transactions and a sink call; every later transition is
guarded by the token, so a slow worker returning after a takeover
changes nothing. Dead rows do not hold back newer versions.

The claim runs as sluiceway_worker, which is granted only the
scheduling columns and may update only the lease. It cannot read
raw_body.

Queries are generated by sqlc (ADR 1) from its pinned Docker image:
make sqlc, and make sqlc-check in CI.

Checked by mutation. Ignoring leases fails four tests. Dropping the
head-of-key rule was missed by the first concurrent FIFO test, which
was rewritten (adjacent versions, in flight from claim time) and now
catches it.

This completes milestone M0.

Closes #4

The first cycle's reviews were deep on isolation, ordering and whether
tests had teeth, because that is what the checklist asked for. It did
not ask for the rest, so nobody looked.

Every review now covers nine dimensions and shows them in a coverage
table in the review body, so a dimension with no findings still says
what was checked: acceptance, tests with teeth, test comprehensiveness
(error paths, boundaries, negative cases, coverage of changed code),
correctness, security (isolation, ordering and secrets as before, plus
injection, input limits, crypto, authorization, dependencies),
performance (with evidence: EXPLAIN on a realistic table, a benchmark,
or a filled-in complexity argument), dead code, codebase improvement
(each with a stated cost), and documentation (architecture, ADRs,
backlog, README status, operator-facing docs, doc comments, the pull
request description).

Severity is spelled out per dimension. The implementer reviews its own
change along the same dimensions before opening the pull request.
